sentences.text: Here, however, one circumstance must not be left out of account, a circumstance which does indeed weaken the disadvantage arising from the lack of genuine grammatical forms in languages, and which could be regarded as a victorious objection to what has just been said.
Even if a grammatical form possesses no designation in the language, it is nevertheless present, as a guiding law of understanding, in those who speak the language.

At the same time it is also, in whatever manner this may be, indicated in some way in the language itself, and it can therefore even seem doubtful whether it is to be ascribed to the language or denied to it, since by language one understands, after all, not merely the dead sounds but the apprehension of them by those who speak.
It remains no less necessary on that account, however, to distinguish this apprehension precisely from the dead sounds, and to speak here solely of what actually lies in the sensible sound.

By grammatical form I therefore understand here an indication of the grammatical relation, in the audible part of the language itself, that is so fixed and pure that the grammatical relation indicated is determinately recognized in it, and that the manner of indication cannot be taken for a designation of a concept at all, but immediately, through itself, makes manifest the difference between the designation of concepts and the designation of relations.

On the manner of indication I can, in keeping with the order deliberately chosen (134.), explain myself only in what follows; here I do not exclude even indication by word order, provided that it is absolutely fixed, immovable, and related to a fixed point that is not itself in turn recognizable only by its position.

If I now assume the case that such an indication of a grammatical form as the one just described is entirely lacking in a language, or is effected not formally but by means of a material concept [Sachbegriff], the form is nonetheless carried into the language all the same, and thus also acts back again from the language upon the soul.
Thus in Chinese, for example, there is no designation of the verb as a grammatical form.
But the language possesses words which, although grammatically they could also be nouns, are always taken in the language only as verbs.

The Chinese speaker therefore never sees in such a word anything other than a verb, and for him the language accordingly has verbs, provided only that one does not attend to whether the verbal nature lies in a grammatical designation or in the habit of linguistic usage.
The same is found where a word in Chinese can be used as a noun just as well as it can as a verb, but the connection of the sense, or the position, indicates that the latter is to be the case.
Yet position in Chinese is not an indication of grammatical form in the sense just established, if only because it lacks a fixed centre outside itself.
It happens further in languages that what were originally material words [Sachwörter] pass over into real relational words [Verhältnisswörter].
In Chinese, ì is a verb and has the meaning of to use, to apply.

But it also serves as a preposition, and Mr Abel-Rémusat observes very rightly that the nation which often has the word on its lips in this latter meaning gradually forgets the original verbal sense entirely.
Here, admittedly, this forgetting becomes more difficult, since the word still has currency as a verb even today.

Yet so often the case is such that the original material meaning has perished entirely and can scarcely still be recognized etymologically, and then such a grammatical word acts merely as a relational concept.

This, however, can have come about only little by little, in gradual transition, and so it is no longer always possible to tell from the language alone what is taken as truly grammatical, as a genuine and pure designation of relation; for that, one would have to know the nation's mode of apprehension, and know it in different epochs.

candidates.author_footnote_translation: Lettre sur le génie de la langue Chinoise à Monsieur Abel Remusat [Letter on the Genius of the Chinese Language, to Monsieur Abel Remusat], p. 22. [editor's callout 1] 98.

uncertainties.issue: 'siegreicher Einwand' is rendered literally. The modality 'angesehen werden könnte' is kept as 'could be regarded', so the objection is entertained and not endorsed.
alternatives: a victorious objection
a decisive objection
a conclusive objection

uncertainties.issue: 'wie es auch sey' may qualify the manner of indication, or it may be a general concessive. 'In der letztern' is taken as 'in the language', as opposed to 'in those who speak it' in s02.
alternatives: in whatever manner this may be
however that may be
be that as it may

uncertainties.issue: 'derselben' in 'die Auffassung derselben' can be genitive plural (the sounds) or genitive feminine singular (the language). I chose the sounds because s04 sets 'diese Auffassung' against 'den todten Tönen'.
alternatives: the apprehension of them (the sounds) by those who speak
the apprehension of it (the language) by those who speak

uncertainties.issue: 'Auffassung' (s03, s04) and 'Auffassungsweise' (s18) are rendered consistently as 'apprehension' and 'mode of apprehension'. Other renderings shift the stress toward the perceptual or the interpretive.
alternatives: apprehension
conception
construal
the way the speakers take them

uncertainties.issue: The scope of 'gerade' is uncertain: it may focus 'von den todten Tönen' or strengthen the necessity of the distinction as a whole. 'Sinnlichen Laute' is rendered 'sensible sound', meaning perceptible to the senses.
alternatives: to distinguish this apprehension precisely from the dead sounds
precisely to distinguish this apprehension from the dead sounds
sensuous sound
sound as perceived by the senses

uncertainties.issue: 'Andeutung' is rendered 'indication' throughout and 'Bezeichnung' as 'designation', to keep Humboldt's two terms distinct. The referent of 'darin' is either the indication or the audible part of the language. 'Bestimmt' may mean 'determinately' or 'with certainty'.
alternatives: recognized in it (the indication)
recognized there (in the audible part of the language)
determinately recognized
definitely recognized

uncertainties.issue: '(134.)' is reproduced as printed. It is presumably an internal cross-reference to a numbered section, but the packet does not confirm this, so it is not expanded to '§134'. The plain 'explain myself' is my choice for 'mich erklären', which could also be 'declare myself'.

'sich auf einen festen, nicht wieder nur an seiner Stellung erkenntlichen Punkt beziehend' is read as: word order counts only if it relates to a fixed point that is identifiable by something other than position alone. The negation scopes over 'only by its position'.
alternatives: a fixed point that is not itself in turn recognizable only by its position
a fixed point not again identifiable merely through its place

uncertainties.issue: The referent of 'sie' in 'so wird sie ... hineingetragen' is ambiguous between 'eine solche Andeutung' and 'grammatische Form'. I resolved it as 'the form', because an indication assumed to be wholly lacking cannot be carried in, and the adjacent §148 says the speaker puts the concept of grammatical relations into the language. This is an interpretive resolution made explicit in the English.
alternatives: the form is nonetheless carried into the language
it is nonetheless carried into the language (ambiguity left open)
the indication is nonetheless carried into the language

uncertainties.issue: 'Sachbegriff' (with 'Sachwörter' in s13 and 'Sachbedeutung' in s17) is rendered with 'material', and the German is given in brackets at first occurrence. The contrast is with 'Verhältniss-' (relational). 'Seele' is rendered 'soul'; 'mind' is the common modernizing alternative.
alternatives: material concept
concept of a thing
object concept
soul
mind

uncertainties.issue: 'Nomina' in early nineteenth-century usage can cover substantives and adjectives together. 'Nouns' may therefore be narrower than Humboldt's term. The comma-isolated 'grammatisch' is taken as 'as far as grammar goes'.
alternatives: nouns
nomina
nominal words

uncertainties.issue: 'Der Chinese' is a generic singular. 'The Chinese speaker' avoids the English ambiguity of 'the Chinese' but adds 'speaker'. 'Für ihn' is kept as 'for him'. The condition 'wenn man nur nicht darauf achtet' restricts the claim that the language has verbs and is kept as a proviso.
alternatives: The Chinese speaker
The Chinese
A Chinese

uncertainties.issue: 'Zusammenhang des Sinnes' may be the connection of the sense or, more loosely, the context. 'Dass das Letztere geschehen soll' is literally 'that the latter is to happen', that is, that the word is to be used as a verb.
alternatives: the connection of the sense
the context of meaning
that the latter is to be the case
that the latter use is intended

uncertainties.issue: 'schon darum ... weil' is rendered 'if only because', which leaves room for other reasons without stating them. 'Ihr' and 'ausser ihr' refer to 'die Stellung' (position), not to the language.
alternatives: if only because it lacks a fixed centre outside itself
for the very reason that it lacks a fixed centre outside itself

uncertainties.issue: 'ì' reproduces the coordinator's reading of an accented italic i in the 1906 print. I have not seen the image, so the accent (grave or another mark) is unverified. It is Humboldt's historical transcription, not modern pinyin. No Chinese character or modern reading is supplied.
alternatives: ì (as read by the coordinator)
another accented form of i, if the print is read differently

uncertainties.issue: 'Herr Abel-Rémusat' is rendered 'Mr Abel-Rémusat'. The present tense 'vergisst' is kept as a generic 'forgets'. It could describe a general tendency of any nation in this situation or the Chinese nation specifically. 'Bedeutung' here refers to the prepositional use and is kept as 'meaning'. The packet does not show where in the main text the author's footnote is anchored. I assume it attaches to this sentence, but no marker is inserted in the translation.
alternatives: Mr Abel-Rémusat
M. Abel-Rémusat
Herr Abel-Rémusat
gradually forgets
comes gradually to forget

uncertainties.issue: 'Allein so oft ist der Fall so' is rendered literally as 'Yet so often the case is such'. 'So oft' may be simply intensive ('very often'). 'Wirkt' is 'acts' or 'operates', and its implied object (the mind or the understanding) is not stated in the source.
alternatives: Yet so often the case is such that
But very often it is the case that
acts merely as a relational concept
functions merely as a relational concept

uncertainties.issue: In 'nicht immer allein mehr der Sprache ansehen', I take 'nicht immer' as 'not always', 'allein' as modifying 'der Sprache' ('from the language alone') and 'mehr' as 'any longer'. 'Wahrhaft grammatisch' may be predicative ('taken as truly grammatical') or adverbial ('taken in a truly grammatical way'). 'Müsste' is kept as the counterfactual 'would have to'.
alternatives: what is taken as truly grammatical, as a genuine and pure designation of relation
what is taken in a truly grammatical way, as a genuine and pure designation of relation

uncertainties.issue: The French title is kept as printed, including 'Chinoise' and the unaccented, unhyphenated 'Abel Remusat', with an English gloss in brackets. The packet does not establish the work's identity or authorship beyond this wording. The terminal '98.' is left uninterpreted, as instructed. The editor's note ('1) Vgl. oben S. 268.', that is, 'Cf. above, p. 268.') belongs to the 1906 edition and is not part of the author's footnote; only its callout position is marked.
alternatives: retain the French title with a bracketed English gloss
retain the French title only
normalize the name to Abel-Rémusat

sentences.text: But a circumstance must not be left out of account here which admittedly weakens the disadvantage of the lack of genuine grammatical forms in languages and could be regarded as a victorious objection to what has just been said.
Even if a grammatical form possesses no designation in the language, it is nonetheless present, as a guiding law of understanding, in those who speak the language.

At the same time it is also in the latter, however it may be, indicated in some way or other, and it may therefore even seem doubtful whether it is to be ascribed to the language or denied to it, since by language one understands not merely the dead sounds, but their apprehension by those who are speaking.
It remains no less necessary for that reason, however, to distinguish this apprehension precisely from the dead sounds, and to speak here only of what really lies in the sensible sound.

By grammatical form I therefore understand here an indication of the grammatical relation in the audible part of language itself so firm and pure that the indicated grammatical relation is determinately recognized in it, and the manner of indication cannot at all be taken for a designation of a concept, but directly makes manifest, through itself, the difference between designation of concepts and designation of relations.

On the manner of indication I can, in accordance with the order deliberately chosen (134.), explain myself only in what follows; here I do not exclude even that by word-order, if it is absolutely firm, immovable, and relates to a fixed point which is not in turn recognizable only from its position.

If I now assume the case that such an indication of a grammatical form as has just been described is entirely lacking in a language, or takes place not formally but through a concept of a thing, it is nevertheless for that reason carried into the language, and thus also acts back again from the language upon the soul.
Thus, for example, in Chinese there is no designation of the verb as a grammatical form.
But the language possesses words which, although grammatically they could also be nouns, are always taken in the language only as verbs.

The Chinese therefore never sees in such a word anything other than a verb, and for him the language accordingly has verbs, if one only does not pay attention to whether the verbal nature lies in a grammatical designation or in the habit of linguistic usage.
The same is found where a word in Chinese can be used just as well like a noun as like a verb, but the coherence of the sense or the position indicates that the latter is to take place.
Yet position in Chinese is already for that reason not an indication of grammatical form in the sense just established, because it lacks a fixed central point outside itself.
It further happens in languages that original words for things pass over into real words of relation.
In Chinese ì is a verb and has the meaning of to use, to employ.

But it also serves as a preposition, and Herr Abel-Rémusat remarks very correctly that the nation which often has the word on its lips in this latter meaning gradually forgets the original verbal sense entirely.
Here, to be sure, this forgetting becomes more difficult, since the word still has currency as a verb even today.

But so often the case is such that the original meaning as to a thing has entirely perished, is hardly still recognizable etymologically, and then such a grammatical word acts merely as a concept of relation.

Meanwhile this could have happened only gradually, in a gradual transition, and it can therefore no longer always be seen from the language alone what is truly taken grammatically, as a genuine and pure designation of relation; for that one would have to know the nation's mode of apprehension, and that in different epochs.

candidates.author_footnote_translation: Lettre sur le génie de la langue Chinoise à Monsieur Abel Remusat. p. 22. [editor callout 1] 98.

uncertainties.issue: In 'so wird sie ... in die Sprache hineingetragen', the pronoun 'sie' is understood as the grammatical form, but its relation to 'Andeutung' in the same sentence leaves the carried-in entity not wholly explicit. 'Sachbegriff' is also conceptually compressed.

sentences.text: Here, however, one circumstance must not be overlooked: it does indeed lessen the disadvantage arising from the lack of genuine grammatical forms in languages, and might be regarded as a decisive objection to what has just been said.
Even if a grammatical form has no designation in the language, it is nevertheless present in those who speak the language, as a guiding law of understanding.

At the same time, it is nevertheless also indicated in the language itself in some way, whatever that way may be; consequently, it may even seem doubtful whether it should be attributed to the language or denied to it, since by language we understand not merely the dead sounds, but also the speakers’ apprehension of them.
Yet it remains no less necessary on that account to distinguish this apprehension precisely from the dead sounds, and here to speak only of what actually lies in the sound perceptible to the senses.

By grammatical form, therefore, I here understand an indication of the grammatical relation in the audible part of language itself that is so fixed and pure that the grammatical relation indicated is distinctly recognized in it, and the manner of indication cannot possibly be taken as a designation of a concept, but immediately, through itself, makes manifest the distinction between the designation of concepts and the designation of relations.

Given the order deliberately chosen (§134), I can explain the manner of indication only later; here I do not even exclude indication through word order, provided that it is absolutely fixed, immovable, and refers to a fixed point that is not itself recognizable merely by its position.

If I now assume a case in which an indication of a grammatical form such as that just described is entirely absent from a language, or is effected not formally but through a concept of a thing, the grammatical form is nevertheless brought into the language and thus also acts back upon the soul from the language.
Thus, for example, in Chinese there is no designation of the verb as a grammatical form.
But the language possesses words which, although grammatically they could also be nouns, are always taken only as verbs in the language.

The Chinese speaker thus never sees anything other than a verb in such a word, and for him the language consequently has verbs, provided one pays no attention to whether their verbal nature lies in a grammatical designation or in habitual linguistic usage.
The same is found where a word in Chinese can be used equally well as a noun or as a verb, but the context of meaning or its position indicates that the latter use is intended.
Yet position in Chinese fails to constitute an indication of grammatical form in the sense just established, if only because it lacks a fixed central point outside itself.
It also happens in languages that words originally denoting things pass into actual words denoting relations.
In Chinese, ì is a verb and means to use, to employ.
But it also serves as a preposition, and Mr Abel-Rémusat very rightly observes that the nation, frequently using the word in this latter meaning, gradually forgets its original verbal sense entirely.
In this instance, admittedly, such forgetting is more difficult, since the word is still current as a verb even today.

But very often the situation is such that the original meaning referring to a thing has disappeared entirely and can scarcely still be discerned even etymologically; in that case, such a grammatical word operates solely as a concept of relation.

Nevertheless, this can only have happened little by little, through a gradual transition, and consequently it is no longer always possible to tell from the language alone what is taken as truly grammatical, as a genuine and pure designation of relation; for that, one would have to know the nation’s manner of apprehension, and to know it at different epochs.

uncertainties.issue: Begriffsbezeichnung and Sachbegriff belong to the passage’s conceptual contrast; their English renderings should not imply a modern linguistic classification.
alternatives: Begriffsbezeichnung: designation of a concept; concept-designation.
Sachbegriff in s07: concept of a thing; substantive concept.

uncertainties.issue: The condition introduced by wenn grammatically refers to indication through word order; its description also directly concerns the fixity of word order itself.
alternatives: Provided that indication through word order is absolutely fixed.
Provided that word order is absolutely fixed.

uncertainties.issue: The pronoun sie can grammatically refer to either Andeutung or grammatische Form. The rendering makes grammatical form explicit because it fits the argument about what speakers bring into language, but the antecedent is not unambiguous.
alternatives: The grammatical form is nevertheless brought into the language.
The indication is nevertheless brought into the language.

uncertainties.issue: The historically printed example is retained as ì. The packet supplies this graphic reading of an accented italic i, but does not establish its character identity or pronunciation.
alternatives: Retain ì as supplied, without assigning a Chinese character or modern reading.

uncertainties.issue: Sachbedeutung continues the contrast between content referring to things and grammatical relation; no single English equivalent preserves its full terminological connection to Sachbegriff and Sachwörter.
alternatives: Meaning referring to a thing.
Substantive meaning.
Lexical meaning, though this risks importing a later analytical distinction.
